latest_report.report:
Mt. Bachelor is scheduled to open for the 26/27 winter season on December 4, conditions permitting. As always, we are committed to opening early if snowfall and conditions allow!

Mt. Bachelor's uphill policy takes effect when Mt. Bachelor opens for the 26/27 winter season, at which time a free Uphill Pass & armband are required. Until then, the slopes are uncontrolled and unpatrolled. Please stay away from equipment, crews at work, and infrastructure. Call 911 in the case of an emergency.

Mountain Gateway is open every weekend through Opening Day on December 4. Stop by the Mt. Bachelor Sports Pro Shop, featuring the PNW’s largest selection of premium ski and snowboard gear, great deals, and expert advice. Print your Season Pass at one of our PUBs, and pick up your Seasonal Rentals on the second floor.

Central Cascades.author: Gabriel Coler
Central Cascades.bottom_line:
I often make the joke that Bend is never as excited about backcountry riding as when there is 6 inches of snow on the cinder cone!  Sure enough there is snow in the high country and folks have been getting out sliding around.  The Central Oregon Avalanche Center is scheduled to begin daily avalanche forecasting on December 1.  By no means does this mean that avalanches aren't possible before then.  If you are headed out to make turns or ride in avalanche terrain, you should consider the possibility of avalanches.  This means doing all the same things you should be doing later in the winter:  carrying avalanche rescue gear, using thoughtful travel techniques, and assessing the snowpack.  When the snow is shallow, folks might be looking for where it's blown in a bit to hit the least rocks.  These wind blown deposits can also be the most likely places to find significant avalanches during the early season.  If you are thinking about heading out, check out both our observations page as well as our weather station map for conditions.  

Hopefully the snow will continue to pile up, and we'll have great riding by the time we begin operating.  In the meantime, be careful out there; of avalanches, but maybe more so of rocks, logs and other snow snakes.  Be patient.  Snow is exciting, but even our worst winters are long.  The avalanche center has lots of pre-season events scheduled to help you build enthusiasm for the season!  Here is a link to our events page:  https://coavalanche.org/pages/events.

Newberry.author: Gabriel Coler
Newberry.bottom_line:
The Central Oregon Avalanche Center is scheduled to begin avalanche forecasting on December 1.  Hopefully we'll have enough snow to ride in the monument by then!  For the Paulina zone we issue avalanche forecasts for every Saturday and Sunday, and usually publish a mid-week observation.  As we start getting drips and drabs of early season snow, check out both our observations page as well as our weather station map for conditions.  If we do pick up enough snow for some early season riding, remember that avalanches are possible even in relatively shallow snowpacks.  This means that if there is enough snow to ride a sled, or make good turns, treat your travel as you would mid-winter; carry avalanche rescue gear, use thoughtful travel techniques, and assess the snow conditions.  Places where you'll find the best early season riding like wind blown deposits are also where you are most likely to find avalanches.

During November and December the avalanche center has lots of pre-season events scheduled to help you build enthusiasm for the season!  Here is a link to our events page:  https://coavalanche.org/pages/events.
